title: Carcass, temple, or neither: what the body is
claim: The Naladiyar mostly treats the body as a pot seeping filth from nine openings, a stinking cart for vultures, and a skin bag the dancer leaves behind; seeing it so is meant to cool desire and turn one to renunciation. The Tirumanthiram holds a different view beside an echo of that one. Its chapter on the body's impermanence speaks of death and mourning, and one verse there nearly repeats Naladiyar 26 (167), though the same chapter also calls the body a walled temple (154); the teaching chapter just before it makes the body the temple where Nandi dwells (116). Later tantras build on the temple: the body of flesh is the Lord's shrine (1823), its very form is the Sivalinga and the dance (1726), and those who dismiss the body as மலம் are dull (2137, if மலம் means bodily filth rather than the soul's impurity). In 725 Tirumular tells the change as his own: he once held the body base, then saw that the Highest had made it his temple, and now he tends it. He does not drop the older view: to the unreleased the body is still a prison (1701), and only a jnani's corpse is exempt from the Naladiyar's indifference to the dead body (1910, 1911). Even the Naladiyar values the body as a means: it is rare to obtain and its fruit should be taken (34), as Tirumular nourishes it because without it one cannot attain true knowledge (724). The Thiruppugazh adds a third, unsettled voice. Arunagirinathar shares the Naladiyar's disgust (815 lists gut, fat, bone and blood in a hut of nine gates) and in several songs rejects Tirumular's remedy: the yogi who holds the breath thinking the impermanent flesh will last is a fool (355, against 722), the medicines and yogas tried on the body are an anguish to be given up (815, against 724), and the anxious yoga that will not accept that the body must go should leave him (211, against 570). Yet other songs ask for that very yoga, a body made diamond-hard and steady through the rising breath (471, 517), so what he rejects is an anxious clinging to the body, not bodily yoga as such.
limits: The Naladiyar's body verses mostly serve to cure lust, so each tension holds only if they are read as a verdict on the body itself. 725's 'once' is a turn in the speaker's understanding, not a sign that the tantras are in the order he wrote them, and whether the Naladiyar or the Tirumanthiram borrowed the dancer-in-the-bag verse is not known. Each Thiruppugazh tension holds only if its song is read as rejecting the practice of preserving the body, and the Tirumanthiram verse as promising bodily longevity, not a figure for it.
audit_issue: The 2137-Naladiyar 43 link is weak: after 2136, மலம் is likelier the soul's impurity, and what the great abandon in Naladiyar 43 is மயல் rather than the body as such. Several Thiruppugazh songs also ask for breath yoga outright (82, 94, 188, 416).
audit_corrections: Claim corrected after the second audit for its findings (Arunagirinathar's inconsistency, the impermanence chapter's content, the sense of மலம் in 2137); the corrected text was not re-audited.

title: Leaping past Death
claim: The Kural says the power won by austerity can even leap past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தல், 269); the Naladiyar answers with the same verb that no one here has leapt past Death and escaped, so give your wealth now (6), and that grey hair will surely come (11). The Tirumanthiram holds both views. Several first-tantra verses side with the Naladiyar: Death does not ask whether one is young (255), black hair turns white (192), and a man can die between supper and bed (148, with Kural 336); a verse in the third tantra adds that all who came before have ended (596). The third tantra's yoga sides with the Kural and goes further: those who know the way have no Yama (711), Death's word does not reach the yogi even in dreams (622), and practice undoes grey hair and wrinkles (647, 848, 727). Only once does Tirumular use the disputed verb itself, in the first tantra and against the Naladiyar's use of it: shed your wealth and you may leap past Death (172).
limits: Every tension holds only on a literal reading of Tirumular's promises. Tradition also reads them as freedom from fear of death or from Yama's judgement after death, and on that reading the books need not clash. Kural 269 is itself read literally by Parimelazhagar and figuratively by Kalaignar.
audit_issue: The first-tantra/third-tantra split is loose: 176, in the first tantra's chapter on wealth, already says Yama's messengers do not come near those who think of the Lord. 622 reads more naturally as freedom from Death's threat than as bodily escape, and 192's last line is too obscure to make greying a stated warning.
audit_corrections: Claim corrected after the audit for the errors it found (verse positions, 724's wording, the 'one verb' framing); the corrected text was not re-audited.
